problem.title: Card-fraud scoring service
problem.context: A payments company scores 3,000 card transactions per second normally and up to 15,000 during seasonal sales before authorization. Fraudsters adapt within weeks; chargeback labels arrive days to weeks later. Auditors may ask months later why a transaction received its score. Five data scientists and two ML engineers work with an operations team, and there is no ML platform team.

requirements.text: Score every card transaction before the authorization decision, using the cardholder's recent activity (for example, the spending of the last hour and the last day).
Update the model as new confirmed fraud cases arrive.
For any past score, show which model version and which input values produced it.
During a seasonal peak of 15,000 transactions per second, a score comes back within 30 ms at the 99th percentile.
When the scoring service or one of its data sources fails, authorizations go on. The business accepts weaker fraud detection for up to 15 minutes, but no authorization may fail because of scoring.
An auditor asks about a score from up to 13 months ago. Within one working day the team answers with the model version, the input values and the training data that model was built from.
When the fraud loss rate rises in one segment, a retrained model can be in production within 48 hours, after it has been compared with the current model on recent transactions.
Card data must stay inside the company's PCI-certified environment: no external service may process it.
Seven people build and run the system, with no dedicated ML platform team.

points.description: A feature store supplies consistent features to a batch-based training process and a real-time model-serving microservice. An automated model-building pipeline versions data, trains and validates models, deploys multiple versions concurrently, and monitors/logs inputs and predictions; prediction-service performance tests check serving behavior. Trade-off: This supports reproducibility, controlled comparison, and operational visibility, but adds infrastructure and coordination across the feature store, data-version repository, pipeline, serving, monitoring, and testing systems. Batch training may also limit how quickly models incorporate newly arriving data.

A dedicated model-builder component incrementally trains, evaluates, validates, and tests model quality using versioned data from a repository. The resulting single production model is served through a local real-time API, while features remain in general-purpose data stores and production usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness are tracked. Trade-off: This supports iterative updates, reproducibility, and operational visibility without specialized feature-store infrastructure. It gives up built-in feature-management capabilities and deployment redundancy, while incremental training and a single production model may increase sensitivity to data drift or update errors.

An automated pipeline versions data in a repository, builds, trains, evaluates, and validates models, combining batch learning with incremental updates. A feature store supplies shared features to hybrid online/offline serving; multiple model versions run concurrently, with logged inputs and predictions and A/B tests comparing them in production. Trade-off: This enables fresh features, continuous adaptation, reproducibility, and controlled comparison, but adds operational complexity across data management, incremental training, monitoring, and parallel deployments. Multiple live versions can also complicate diagnosis and consistency.

A versioned data repository feeds a feature store and batch training, while an automated pipeline builds, evaluates, validates, and tests model quality. Approved models are served through a real-time microservice, with multiple versions deployed concurrently and monitored for usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, repeatable delivery, controlled comparison, and broad production visibility. It gives up operational simplicity through duplicated model serving, version coordination, monitoring overhead, and potentially stale predictions from batch-trained models.

A local service/API delivers real-time predictions using features retrieved from general-purpose data stores. A dedicated model builder incrementally trains, evaluates, and validates models; data versions and trained-model quality are recorded, production behavior is tracked, and rollback redeploys a previous model when needed. Trade-off: This provides rapid model updates, traceability, operational visibility, and recovery, but generic feature storage may lack ML-specific support, while incremental training and local serving increase operational complexity.

The system uses a feature store to support both batch and online features, with model factors trained through a combination of automated batch pipelines and incremental updates. Versioned data and pipeline validation produce deployable models; multiple versions serve concurrently for A/B testing, while production data and predictions are logged for monitoring. Trade-off: This supports experimentation, fresh personalization, reproducibility, and gradual comparison of models, but increases coordination and operational complexity across batch and online paths. Multiple versions and incremental training also raise risks of feature, data, and model inconsistency and increase storage and monitoring costs.

The system stores features in general-purpose data stores, versions datasets in a dedicated repository, and uses an automated pipeline for batch training, evaluation, validation, and evidence-based hypothesis testing. A locally hosted API serves predictions, while production tracking monitors usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness; if needed, operators redeploy a previous model version. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, auditability, observability, and recoverability. It gives up specialized feature-store capabilities and rapid adaptation from batch training, potentially increasing operational burden for local serving and monitoring.

A versioned data repository feeds a feature store used by a real-time model-serving microservice. An automated pipeline trains and validates batch and incrementally updated model factors, deploys multiple versions concurrently, and uses performance tests plus production tracking to monitor behavior, usage, inputs, outputs, interpretability, and fairness. Trade-off: This supports low-latency serving, continual adaptation, reproducibility, and controlled model comparison, but increases operational complexity and resource costs. Maintaining consistency across batch and online features, incremental training, multiple deployed versions, and their monitoring and tests also creates additional failure and governance risks.

A local service/API serves real-time predictions, using features stored in general-purpose data stores and models trained through a hybrid batch/incremental process. A dedicated model-builder component trains and validates models, a data-version repository supports reproducibility, production tracking monitors behavior and fairness, and rollback redeploys a previous model when needed. Trade-off: This gains responsive serving, flexible updating, traceability, and operational recovery, but hybrid training and generic feature storage increase integration and consistency complexity, while model-quality tests and monitoring may leave broader pipeline failures uncovered.

1. **Solution:** A feature store supports both online service computations and offline batch jobs, while hybrid training updates some model factors in batches and others incrementally. An automated pipeline uses repository-versioned data for training, evaluation, validation, and A/B testing; production tracking monitors behavior, and rollback redeploys a prior model when needed. 2. **Trade-off:** This gains reproducibility, deployment safety, flexible serving, and visibility into production behavior. It gives up operational simplicity: online/offline consistency, coordinated batch and incremental training, feature-store management, experimentation, and multiple model versions require additional infrastructure and governance.

The system serves predictions through a local real-time API, reading features from general-purpose data stores. A model-building pipeline uses versioned data for evidence-based testing, combines batch and incremental training, tracks production behavior, and supports redeploying a prior model version when needed. Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, operational visibility, and recovery while supporting both offline and online learning. It gives up the convenience of specialized feature-store capabilities and adds complexity in coordinating hybrid training, versioned data, monitoring, and rollback.

approaches.idea: What if a feature store and automated batch pipeline anchor a real-time microservice with concurrent model versions?
What if a locally hosted API, general-purpose feature stores, and incremental learning keep deployment lean and responsive?
What if a feature store and hybrid online/offline serving support hybrid learning and direct A/B comparison?
What if a local API and general-purpose feature storage keep the runtime simple, with versioned batch training and rollback?

trajectory.hypothesis: A real-time microservice and feature store can serve recent activity; a batch pipeline and dataset versions aid repeatability, while concurrent versions and performance tests help compare and validate releases.

tradeoffs.note: Batch training and versioned inputs support reproducibility but wait for chargeback labels and a training run before adapting.

trajectory.observation: The checked combination is valid but unattested. The serving and feature choices align with online scoring, while batch learning limits the pace of model refresh. The point descriptions do not establish numeric latency or fail-open behavior.

trajectory.hypothesis: A local API and incremental learning should favor prompt scoring and updates; tracking inputs and model behavior with versioned data supports audit reconstruction.

tradeoffs.note: Incremental learning can incorporate confirmed cases promptly but complicates reproducible training snapshots and controlled release comparison.
One production model reduces deployment overhead but offers no concurrent comparison path.

trajectory.observation: The point is valid and unattested. Input and model tracking provide a stronger audit trail, but the chosen single-model deployment does not directly compare a candidate against the current model.

trajectory.hypothesis: Hybrid serving and learning with a feature store should combine fresh online features and offline processing; A/B testing concurrent models should support the required recent comparison.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid online/offline paths support fresh scoring and adaptation but add work whose peak latency remains unproven.

trajectory.observation: This combination makes the comparison workflow explicit and supports more frequent updates, at the cost of the broadest operational surface. Its data logging does not yet explicitly describe the model version and all input values needed for an audit response.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace generic logging with model in-production tracking and add trained-model quality tests to improve traceability while retaining the batch pipeline and online service.

tradeoffs.note: Batch-based training yields repeatable data and model artifacts but cannot guarantee fast adaptation to delayed labels.

trajectory.observation: Tracking broadens the production record to model usage and inputs, and quality tests strengthen candidate checks. The point remains unattested; the training-data retention period and 13-month retrieval workflow are not specified by the values.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keep local incremental serving and explicit input tracking, and change single-model production to rollback support so an unsuccessful update can be reversed.

tradeoffs.note: Frequent updates help adaptation but training snapshots must be preserved separately for reliable historical reconstruction.

trajectory.observation: Rollback adds an explicit recovery path and the production tracker captures inputs and usage. A candidate comparison and rollback procedure still need to be provided around these values.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use production tracking for model and input details and code-repository data versioning, retaining hybrid serving, training, and A/B testing.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid paths and concurrent models support comparison but increase serving complexity that must still meet the latency target.

trajectory.observation: Model and input tracking improves the audit path, though code-repository data versioning may be less convenient for large training datasets. The point is still unattested.

trajectory.hypothesis: A locally hosted API with general feature stores, batch pipeline, evidence-based testing, and rollback may offer a lower-complexity starting point while retaining audit records and controlled releases.

tradeoffs.note: Batch updates improve repeatability but respond more slowly to delayed confirmed labels.
General-purpose storage avoids specialized feature-store operations but leaves recent-feature consistency and access behavior to the team.

trajectory.observation: This approach combines local control and rollback with a batch workflow; its simpler serving stack gives up specialized feature support and rapid adaptation. The checked point is valid but unattested.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace batch-only learning with hybrid batch and incremental learning to improve adaptation while retaining feature consistency, version tracking, multiple releases, and performance tests.

tradeoffs.note: Incremental updates improve adaptation, while the added training path needs validation against the peak latency budget.

trajectory.observation: The combined training mode improves the adaptation hypothesis while the performance test remains relevant to the peak target. No point description or evidence establishes that the 30 ms target is achieved.

trajectory.hypothesis: Use hybrid rather than only incremental training so model factors can receive repeatable batch validation as well as updates, while retaining local serving and rollback.

tradeoffs.note: Hybrid training improves responsiveness but coordinating its feature paths adds work before the latency target is established.

trajectory.observation: Hybrid learning retains fast adaptation while restoring batch validation opportunities. The point supports candidate evaluation conceptually but does not quantify the 48-hour delivery cycle.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replace concurrent production versions with rollback to test whether a recovery-oriented release path reduces the operational burden while retaining hybrid serving, learning, and A/B evaluation.

tradeoffs.note: Rollback offers a contained recovery path with less concurrent runtime overhead, but candidate comparison requires additional evaluation machinery.

trajectory.observation: The rollback variant is valid and unattested. It may reduce concurrent serving overhead but weakens the direct production comparison path; A/B testing still requires a controlled way to compare the candidate with recent transactions.

trajectory.hypothesis: Change batch-only learning to hybrid learning to improve updates without changing the local API, general feature storage, rollback, and evidence-based testing.

tradeoffs.note: Online/offline serving and training support responsive scoring and updates, but the more complex path has unproven peak latency.

trajectory.observation: The change improves adaptability while preserving the locally controlled runtime. Evidence-based testing still needs to be operationalized as a comparison against recent transactions.
